newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Britain's Major sees way forward in European IGC.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Major sees way forward in European IGC.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major said on Sunday he could see a way to break the deadlock on one of the key issues preventing progress on the European Union's overhaul of its treaties and institutions.

But he sent a signal to Germany and France that they would have to compromise to get a deal in Europe's Intergovernmental Conference (IGC) on the key issue of "flexibility", seen as essential if Europe is to take on new members.

Major's confidence on getting a deal on "flexibility" -- European jargon for letting groups of states within the union forge ahead together on matters where others are less enthusiastic -- follows talks with Dutch prime minister Wim Kok.

Partly due to Britain's increasingly sceptical line on Europe, flexibility has become one of the key points of the IGC debate, with Germany and France wanting to forge ahead on the path towards political union while Britain stands opposed.
Major met Kok last Tuesday on the eve of the British prime minister's week-long tour of India, Pakistan and Bangladesh.
He told reporters travelling with him on Sunday: "I think we can make progress on that (flexibility). The great debate is how flexible it will be and what sort of flexibility it will be...
"I can see a way of unlocking it. We still have to negotiate a way through, but I can see now how it can be done."

But he said, in what was seen as a reference to Germany and France, that the deal would have to be approved not just by the EU presidency, currently held by the Netherlands, but also by other members.

"It will only be enshrined in treaty when the heads of government meet," said Major, who has told reporters repeatedly during the trip that he expects to be at the EU summit in June, which would be after general elections he is forecast to lose.

Major, who is under pressure at home from 'Eurosceptics' in his ruling Conservative party opposed to European integration but who is wary of following them into what he sees as unecessary isolationism, refused to detail the way ahead.

But he rejected a suggestion that he could accept a German-style flexibility deal, which would allow a group of core states to forge on together, using European institutions, without Britain or other states being able to hold them back.

And he gave the clearest of hints that he sees opt-outs, like those he negotiated for Britain from plans for a social chapter setting common labour standards and for a single European currency, as the way forward.
"Some people have opt-outs on monetary union, some people have opt-outs on social affairs. That is going to have to accelerate in future as the European Union enlarges."
Germany and France have already made clear that they want opt-outs to be the exception rather than the rule.
